SENIOR DEDUCTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's the new $6,000 senior deduction worth?

A new federal deduction applies to tax years 2025 through 2028: up to $6,000 for each taxpayer on the return who is age 65 or older — up to $12,000 on a joint return when both spouses qualify — but it shrinks once modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) clears $75,000 (single/HoH/qualifying surviving spouse) or $150,000 (joint), and it is not available at all to married filing separately. This applies the phase-out and the MFS rule and estimates the deduction.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status & income

Married filing separately cannot claim this deduction at all, regardless of age or income — see the result below.

2. Who on this return is 65 or older?

The spouse checkbox only applies on a joint return — it's ignored for every other filing status. Each qualifying person is worth up to $6,000; on a joint return with both boxes checked, that's up to $12,000 combined.

Fill in filing status and MAGI, check who on the return is 65 or older, then click Calculate.

Estimate

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates one deduction only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax.
  • Age and Social Security number are self-reported — this tool does not verify either.
  • Not the existing "extra standard deduction for age" that has applied for years — this is a separate, additional, temporary deduction on top of it.
  • Federal only. Most states still tax the same income in full unless that state separately conforms, and this does not change Social Security's own taxation rules or payroll (FICA/SECA) tax.

2025 federal marginal tax brackets (reference)

For choosing the rate above. Sourced from the IRS's published 2025 brackets; verify current-year brackets before filing, and remember your marginal rate is the rate on your last dollar of income, not your average rate.

Common questions

How much is the new senior tax deduction?

Up to $6,000 per qualifying taxpayer age 65 or older, for tax years 2025 through 2028. On a joint return where both spouses are 65 or older, that is up to $12,000 combined. It phases out at higher incomes -- see the phase-out question below.

Can I claim this if I file married filing separately?

No. Married filing separately is excluded entirely, at any income and regardless of age -- a married couple must file a joint return for either spouse to claim it. This is the SAME direction as this portfolio's own no-tax-on-tips-overtime-calculator, and the OPPOSITE of its auto-loan-interest-deduction-calculator, where MFS is explicitly eligible.

What is the income phase-out?

Each qualifying person's $6,000 is reduced by 6 cents for every dollar that modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $75,000 (single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse) or $150,000 (married filing jointly). It reaches exactly $0 at $175,000 MAGI (single/HoH/QSS) or $250,000 MAGI (joint) -- the same joint zero-crossing point whether one or two spouses qualify, since each person's $6,000 phases out independently against the same household MAGI.

Do I have to itemize to claim it?

No. This deduction stacks on top of the standard deduction (and the existing extra standard deduction for age) whether you itemize or not -- it is not an itemized deduction.

Is this permanent?

No. Under current law it applies to tax years 2025, 2026, 2027, and 2028 only, and expires afterward unless a future law extends it.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory amount, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers and checkboxes you enter. It is not a full tax return, it does not verify your age or Social Security number, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own age, Social Security number status, and MAGI before filing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also planning around a new car loan or claiming "no tax on tips/overtime"? See the auto loan interest deduction calculator (note it treats married filing separately the OPPOSITE way this one does) and the tips & overtime deduction calculator (MFS excluded there too, same as here). Still have 401(k) after-tax headroom to use? See the mega backdoor Roth calculator — a separate, stackable move from this deduction. Itemizing in a high-tax state instead? See the SALT deduction cap calculator — another new 2025 MAGI-based phase-out, but one that floors at a fixed dollar amount rather than phasing fully to zero like this one.

Estimating this by hand instead? See where a hand calculation of this deduction usually goes wrong. Wondering at what income this stops helping at all? See at what income does the senior deduction phase out completely?

vs-estimating-the-deduction-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. doing it by hand

The new $6,000 senior deduction looks like simple arithmetic -- an amount, a phase-out, an eligibility check. The problem is that this portfolio now has three 2025 OBBBA deductions with different rules for the same two questions (does MFS qualify, does the phase-out round in steps), and a quick by-hand estimate tends to carry the wrong sibling's answer over.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Married filing separatelyAssumes MFS gets a reduced amount, generalizing from this portfolio's own auto-loan-interest-deduction-calculator (where MFS IS eligible, with its own cap).Excludes MFS entirely and says so plainly, rather than computing a partial amount.
Confusing it with the existing age-65 standard deduction add-onTreats the new $6,000 as replacing, or double-counting with, the existing extra standard deduction for age that is already on Form 1040.Computes this deduction as an amount that stacks on top of the standard deduction (and its existing age add-on), never as a replacement for either.
The MAGI phase-out step sizeRounds the excess MAGI to the nearest $1,000, generalizing from this portfolio's own stepped-rounding sibling deductions.Applies a continuous 6 cents per dollar of MAGI over the threshold, with no rounding step.
Two qualifying spouses on a joint returnAssumes the combined $12,000 phases out as one pot, rather than each spouse's $6,000 phasing out independently against the same MAGI excess.Computes each qualifying person's $6,000 and its own reduction separately, then sums the result.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake estimating this deduction by hand?

Assuming married filing separately gets a reduced amount, generalizing from this portfolio's own auto-loan-interest-deduction-calculator, where MFS is explicitly eligible with its own cap. This deduction excludes MFS entirely -- $0, at any income or age -- a married couple must file a joint return for either spouse to claim any of it.

What's the second most common mistake?

Confusing this with the existing extra standard deduction for age 65+ that has been on Form 1040 for years. This is a separate, new, additional deduction -- it stacks ON TOP of that existing age-based amount and the regular standard deduction, not instead of either one.

How does the MAGI phase-out usually get estimated wrong?

By assuming it rounds in $1,000 steps the way this portfolio's own auto-loan and tips/overtime deductions do. This one does not -- it is a continuous 6 cents per dollar of MAGI over the threshold, with no rounding step at all, so $100,001 and $100,999 of excess MAGI cost two different amounts, not the same amount.

On a joint return where both spouses qualify, does the combined $12,000 phase out as one pot?

No, and assuming so is an easy by-hand mistake. Each spouse's own $6,000 phases out independently against the same household MAGI excess. It happens to reach exactly $0 at the same MAGI either way ($250,000 joint) -- but the deduction at any MAGI between the threshold and that point is not simply double a one-spouse estimate.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, or state conformity. Both apply the same published federal amount, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers you enter; verify against the IRS's own guidance or a qualified tax professional before filing.

This page names no specific product or service -- it compares against the generic method of estimating the deduction by hand, not a competing tool.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply the published federal statutory amount, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own age, Social Security number status, and MAGI before filing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

why-does-the-senior-deduction-phase-out-.text:
← back to the calculator

At what income does the senior deduction phase out completely?

$175,000 MAGI (single, head of household, qualifying surviving spouse) or $250,000 MAGI (married filing jointly) -- always exactly $100,000 above the phase-out threshold.

That $100,000 is not a separate, arbitrarily chosen number. It falls out of the other two numbers the statute already sets: a $6,000-per-person deduction reduced by 6 cents for every dollar of MAGI over the threshold. $6,000 ÷ 0.06 = $100,000 -- the exact amount of income headroom it takes to erase one person's deduction at that rate.

The two thresholds, and where each one zeroes out

Filing statusPhase-out startsFully phased out
Single / head of household / qualifying surviving spouse$75,000 MAGI$175,000 MAGI
Married filing jointly$150,000 MAGI$250,000 MAGI

Worked examples along the phase-out

A single filer, one qualifying person, at four different MAGI levels:

MAGIExcess over $75,000Reduction (6% of excess)Deduction
$100,000$25,000$1,500$4,500
$150,000$75,000$4,500$1,500
$175,000 or more$100,000+$6,000 (capped)$0

Two qualifying spouses don't need a higher income to zero out

It is tempting to assume a joint return with two qualifying spouses -- up to $12,000 of deduction instead of $6,000 -- would need twice the MAGI headroom to phase out completely. It does not, because each spouse's own $6,000 phases out independently against the same household MAGI excess:

Joint return, MAGIQualifying spousesCombined deduction
$150,000 (at the threshold)2$12,000
$200,0002$6,000
$250,0002$0
$250,0001$0

Both the one-qualifying-spouse and two-qualifying-spouse joint returns reach $0 at the identical $250,000 MAGI -- the phase-out rate applies per-person, but the household MAGI it is tested against is the same number either way.

Not a cliff, unlike this portfolio's auto loan deduction

This portfolio's own auto loan interest deduction calculator rounds the MAGI excess up to the next $1,000 before applying its $200-per-$1,000 reduction -- so $100,001 of MAGI there already costs as much as $100,999 does. The senior deduction's 6%-per-dollar rate has no such rounding step: one extra dollar of MAGI here costs six-tenths of one cent, smoothly, all the way to the $100,000-wide phase-out range.

Common questions

At what MAGI does the senior deduction reach $0?

$175,000 MAGI for single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse filers. $250,000 MAGI for married filing jointly. Both numbers are the phase-out threshold plus exactly $100,000.

Why $100,000 above the threshold specifically?

The deduction phases out at 6 cents per dollar of MAGI over the threshold, and the deduction itself is $6,000 per qualifying person. $6,000 divided by 0.06 is $100,000 -- the exact amount of MAGI headroom it takes to erase one person's $6,000 at a 6-cent-per-dollar rate.

Does the deduction phase out slower when both spouses qualify?

No. Each spouse's own $6,000 phases out independently against the same household MAGI excess, so a two-qualifying-spouse joint return reaches $0 at the identical $250,000 MAGI a one-qualifying-spouse joint return does -- it does not take a higher income to zero out twice as much deduction.

Is the phase-out a cliff, like the auto loan interest deduction's rounding rule?

No. The auto loan interest deduction rounds the MAGI excess up to the next $1,000 before applying its reduction, which can nudge the answer by up to $200 at an unlucky dollar amount. This deduction's 6%-per-dollar rate is continuous -- one extra dollar of MAGI costs six-tenths of one cent, not a jump to the next bracket.

Does this deduction stack with the extra standard deduction for being 65 or older?

Yes. This is a separate, additional deduction on top of both the regular standard deduction and the existing extra standard-deduction amount for taxpayers 65 and older. It is available whether you itemize or take the standard deduction.

Run your own numbers

The senior deduction calculator applies this same phase-out to your own MAGI and filing status, for one or two qualifying spouses. Nothing you enter is uploaded.
